vignette: Malik grew up in a dimly lit apartment where the only rule was silence. His stepfather’s rage never came with warning. It arrived as the heavy, measured rhythm of boots on hardwood, the sudden drop of temperature against Malik’s bare feet when he was dragged from his bed, and the coarse, scratchy weave of the hallway rug that scraped his palms as he tried to crawl away. Those sensory anchors became hardwired. Years later, a draft off a subway grate or the click of a cab door locking still pulls his breath short, because his nervous system never learned that the danger belonged to the past. As a teenager, Malik found that every time a car door slammed nearby or the weather turned damp and cold against his skin, his shoulders seized and his eyes tracked every shadow. The sensations didn’t just startle him; they convinced him that he was perpetually exposed. He stopped taking rides on crowded buses, began driving recklessly down empty highways just to outrun the panic, and learned to ignore anyone who told him to breathe or slow down. His body felt like a traitor, constantly sounding alarms in empty rooms, which only deepened his conviction that he was fundamentally fractured. He was sure he had been permanently altered, that the soft boy he used to be was gone, replaced by someone who could never truly relax. Each night he spent alone on his couch, scrolling past other people’s lives and letting the pills dull the ache in his chest, only proved to him that he was incapable of real connection. The distance he kept from friends and family wasn’t just preference; it was a self-fulfilling prophecy that solidified his belief that he had permanently changed for the worse and severed his ties to his community. Now, at twenty-seven, Malik spends fourteen hours a day in the confined cabin of his rental car, weaving through Atlanta’s grid. The job should have been a sanctuary of controlled distance, but it became a mirror for his own hyperarousal. When a passenger’s heavy boots clicked on the pavement as they approached the curb, Malik’s hands tightened on the wheel and his eyes darted to the rearview mirror. That familiar spike of dread didn’t just make him watchful; it made him feel exposed, as if the past were tracking him through the glass. To survive the shift, he reached for the strategies that had kept him alive: he scrolled through racing streams until his vision blurred, popped pills to quiet the ringing in his ears, and deliberately pulled passengers who asked for long rides just to avoid small talk. The work demanded steady hands, but his chronic alertness and need to stay ahead of perceived threats left him exhausted and irritable. He took corners too fast, braked late, and rationalized it as staying sharp, but the recklessness only reinforced his fear that he could never truly trust his own safety or anyone else’s reassurance. He felt permanently changed, a man whose body would never stop bracing, and the distance he maintained from passengers and strangers alike only widened the gap between him and the community he once called home. The cycle tightened over the years. His withdrawal made him more sensitive to ordinary stimuli; a sudden cold draft in the cab or the thump of a bass line from a passing SUV would instantly flood him with the same visceral alarm, which in turn made his body brace harder and his judgment blur. He told himself he was broken beyond repair, that his isolation was just proof he didn’t belong anywhere anymore, but the mounting tension in his chest finally outweighed the pride. After nearly causing a three-car pileup when a pedestrian stepped off the curb and his gas pedal stuck under his own panic, Malik handed in his keys. He sat in a clinic waiting room now, gripping a coffee cup that felt too cold, terrified that he was beyond saving, yet quietly hoping someone might finally help him untangle the wire from the wire.
